Author: @panda4247
Content:
This seems very incomplete.
Yes, it's a short video, but I would skip the part about the poles and talk more about the height where you want to go..
The point, is, you can't just be "as high and fast as a satellite" compared to any random satellite. If you are as high as most satellites (low earth orbit), you would need to go much faster than you are standing on the ladder. The satellites in LEO have period around once every 1.5 hours (i.e. you would need to go ~16 times faster than you are, thus you would fall down)
The height you'd need to climb in order to not fall down is the one, where you can stay in orbit hovering above the exact same spot of the Earth -- which is, you guessed correctly, the Geostationary orbit (some 35.8k km / 22.2k miles above the surface).
If you went still higher up, you would not just fly off to the space and never return, you would just have higher and slower elliptical orbit and return back to that spot (relative to space) in some time... however, since you'd have different period than the Earth, the ladder would not be there :)
You'd have to go much higher...

Author: @generichuman_
Content:
I gave this problem to openai's o1 model. 

To achieve orbit simply by stepping off the top of a ladder, the ladder would need to extend up to the altitude where an object’s tangential speed due to Earth’s rotation matches the orbital speed required at that altitude. This special altitude is known as the geostationary orbit.

At the Earth's surface, the rotational speed (tangential speed due to Earth’s rotation) is about 465 m/s at the equator. This speed is far less than the orbital speed required at low Earth orbit altitudes (approximately 7,800 m/s). As you climb higher, the required orbital speed decreases, while the rotational speed increases (since it’s proportional to the radius from Earth’s center).

At the geostationary orbit radius, which is about 42,164 km from Earth’s center (or approximately 35,786 km above the Earth's surface), the rotational speed matches the required orbital speed. Here, the Earth's rotation is sufficient to keep an object in orbit without any additional speed. 

This can be shown by equating the required centripetal acceleration for circular motion (due to the object's tangential speed from Earth's rotation) to the gravitational acceleration at that altitude:

\[ \omega^2 r = \frac{GM_{\text{Earth}}}{r^2} \]

Solving for \( r \) provides the radius where the gravitational pull equals the centripetal force needed for orbital motion at Earth's rotational speed \( \omega \). This radius corresponds to the geostationary orbit.

Therefore, if you climbed a ladder up to the geostationary orbit altitude of approximately 35,786 km and stepped off, you would be in orbit around Earth, matching Earth’s rotation and remaining above the same point on the equator.

**Answer: About 35,786 km high—the altitude of geostationary orbit where stepping off puts you in orbit.**

Author: @TF2CrunchyFrog
Content:
What the techbros who read about "space elevators" in Scifi novels and got excited are missing, are some crucial details:
1. While it's _technically_ possible, on paper, to design a space elevator, the most glaring problem is: _We don't have any lightweight materials with enough tensile strength for that hypothetical 60+km long cable!_ And it might in fact be impossible in the real world. Every rope or cable has a specific length, depending on its material, its diameter and tensile strength and other physics variables, where it will simply snap _under its own weight,_ before you even put elevator cabins on it!

Also, your magical supermaterial should be impervious to day-and-night cycle heating and cooling, because you really don't want these cables to elongate and shrink again too much!

2. Assuming you found your magical material to magically make 60+km long ropes from it, you now have to anchor one end in the ground, then somehow get the other end ito orbit and tether it there (to an orbital ring you magicall built), with the weight of the rest of the cable between it. Likely by letting down a cable from orbit, then using it to pull up your first cable.

3. Congrats, you now have giant endless cables stretching from the equator to orbit. Wind pressure on these xables, especially at the layer of the jet stream air currents, is enormous. And when they start to vibrate, they will _hum._ And also rip the orbital ring apart. Or rip its anchor from the ground, so you have a giant block of rock swinging around. Cheers!

4. Your "fence" of giant cables is also a real threat to aircraft, other spacecraft, whatever.

5. And should one of those giant cables ever _rip apart,_ be it from material failure (wind pressure, heating, cooling) or terrorist attacks or plain old wars, you now have several dozen kilometers of thick cable falling from orbit, slicing through the air, heating up from air resistance as it whips towards the ground while the planet below rotates. Oh, and on the topic of whips... you do know that whips make that loud snapping sound because the end of a whip's cord moves at supersonic speed, yes? Now imagine that with a 60+km long giant red-hot cable.... before it slams into the ground, obliterating entire cities, forest, agricultural land, damming rivers, creating a cloud of dust and debris. Enjoy.

Author: @prof7304
Content:
The centrifugal acceleration is 
a = v²/r 
The gravitational acceleration equals 
a = 9,81 m/s²

The earth rotates once every 24 hours aka 86,400 seconds. The distance you move during that time is 
s = 2πr 
So the speed you go relative to the radius is 
v = 2πr/86,400s 

Now we can bring the equations together in order to calculate what radius you would need in order to float like a sattelite: 

9,81 m/s² = (2πr/86,400s)²/r 

Meaning 

r = 86,400² 9,81/(4π²) m = 1,854,969,424m 

The earths Radius is 
6,378,000 m 

So you would need to climb the ladder around 
1,850,000,000 m!

Content:
It's important to note that the Earth isn't spinning exactly on its center/core like a car's wheel. The "axis" is actually in the mantle of the Earth, not the core, because of the moon's right gravitational pull. Essentially, imagine mounting the car axle on one of the car on one of the spokes of the aluminum rim.

So, the speed you're traveling depends on whether or not the moon is over your head or not.

Author: @TallinuTV
Content:
"Climbing the ladder into space" _does not_ require "climbing the ladder to geostationary orbit." When you let go, you will go into freefall. But unless you are specifically doing the second one, from a ladder at the equator, you _will_ move away from your starting point. But you might not fall the direction you'd expect. (And not necessarily straight up or down, either, it depends on your latitude and exactly how high you climbed.)

If you climb your ladder PAST geostationary orbit, then you'll find the apparent force to be "pulling you away from the planet" as long as you hold on to the ladder, and it'll start to feel like you're upside down, and if you do let go, you'll find yourself in an elliptic orbit (for a long, _long_ time) which takes you up and away from earth (further depending on just how far you climbed) before returning to the altitude at which you let go.

There are altitudes below geostationary orbit, as well, where if you let go, you will remain in orbit. It still won't be circular, but will instead dip down toward the atmosphere to varying degrees, closer the lower you are when you let go. If you're low enough, you'll dip into the atmosphere and that will slow you down, likely pulling you into lower and lower orbits until you are deep enough in the atmosphere to burn up like a meteor.

At exactly the geostationary altitude on a ladder over the equator, you will simply float approximately where you are if you let go, remaining near the ladder without moving sideways or up or down. You are literally in the same orbit as a large population of communications satellites, though you'd be unlikely to see any without a telescope. (If you have satellite TV, this is the region those satellites are placed in, because your dish can be pointed at one spot in the sky and doesn't have to move to track the satellite.)

If your ladder was not at the equator, and not near either pole, you'll experience a "sideways" force as you climb, and letting go will put you in an inclined orbit that takes you equal parts north and south of the equator (assuming you aren't low enough to reenter and burn up). You will not go any farther north/south than your starting latitude was from the equator, but as the Earth rotates under your orbital track, you'll eventually see every part of it within that range (say, from 40 degrees N to 40 S).

If you're close enough to one pole, your circular path through the sky as Earth turns will not be wide enough to "miss the Earth" as you fall, and so you will simply fall in a parabolic arc, until you reach the atmosphere, and either burn up or hit terminal velocity (and then hit the ground), depending on your latitude and starting altitude.

There you go. Pretty sure that's all your options! ;)

Author: @eyallev
Content:
two mistakes.

first, dropping from 100 km up, MIGHT not cause you to burn up (depending on your mass and profile size), drag will slow you down, to terminal velocity, which is the speed a free falling skydiver goes at (in fact, you might freeze to death, before you get enough friction to slow you down).

second, geostationary orbit is about 30,000 km up, this is where letting go, will having you floating next to the ladder, however even before that height, you would have a "stable" (elliptical) orbit if you let go (the ladder "run" way from you, as you don't have enough speed for a circular orbit, but you will catch up to it on your way down; HOWEVER, even if you don't grab it, you will find yourself at the height you started at (and you'd get there BEFORE the ladder catchs up with you), as long as you stay clear of the atmosphere, you should be able to grab the ladder at least once per "orbit"; if you let go above the 30,000km point, you will still be orbiting earth, but at a slower rate than the ladder (however at the start, you will be going faster than it).

in short, orbital mechanics is strange.

Author: @PauxloE
Content:
Therer are a few problems with the ladder:
→ Don't stop climbing as soon as you are above most of the atmosphere (100 km), or e.g. at the ISS' level (400 km), you'll still plummet to death. You need to go much farther out than that, around 36000 km high (geostationary orbit).
→ We don't have strong enough material yet to build such a long ladder (for Earth – on Mars it's likely easier).
→ You should make sure to bring some oxygen with you, otherwise you'll suffocate.
→ You'll also need to bring enough food (and more oxygen) with you so you can actually climb that high (your muscles need energy for climbing)
→ The oxygen and food will make you heavier, so you need even more oxygen and food to carry that. (And the ladder needs to become a lot sturdier at the bottom to carry us.)
→ (Basically, we again get the rocket equation, just with a bit nicer factors.)

(Of course, you can eliminate part of that by not using your own muscle power for climbing, but e.g. electricity provided by the ladder. Or exchange energy with someone else going downwards.)

Content:
Space elevators are not very efficient. Have to be far higher than just reaching the edge of space, and they have not other use.
What we actually should build are orbital rings. These can be at any height, even inside the atmosphere, and as rings around the planet they have many potential uses.

The key idea is using two rings, one stationary relative to the surface, and one inside it that spins much faster than orbital speed. The outer ring wants to fall down, the inner ring wants to fly out. If they are balanced just right, the whole system is floating without any support. Then you anchor it to the ground at a few places to prevent it from floating away. Attach elevators to the anchor cables, and you can go up and down at will.

The best part is that this can be built today. No special material needed. It doesn't even have to be too expensive, because we can start small, and use the existing ring to lift up more building materials. It's similar to building suspension bridges.

I might add that due to axial precession, you are never quite stationary even when the ladder is placed on one of Earth's poles.

Precession, as you might know, is the movement of Earth's axis over time: Think about a spinning top which wobbles slowly while spinning, which in Earth's case takes about 26 000 years.

Content: To stay afloat straight above the same spot: geostationary orbit, a circular orbit 35,785 km (22,236 miles) above Earth’s Equator in which a satellite’s orbital period is equal to Earth’s rotation period of 23 hours and 56 minutes. A spacecraft in this orbit appears to an observer on Earth to be stationary in the sky. This particular orbit is used for meteorological and communications satellites. The geostationary orbit is a special case of the geosynchronous orbit, which is any orbit with a period equal to Earth’s rotation period.
